mainTopic: The end time of רבי אליעזר's evening שמע, the watches of the night in heaven and on earth, and the story of רבי יוסי in the ruin
overview: The גמרא first deals with two contradictions. רבי מאיר and רבי אליעזר each seem to give two different start times for the evening שמע. It answers that two students reported each sage differently. For רבי אליעזר it adds another answer: the opening of the משנה is not his words. Next it asks why רבי אליעזר said 'until the end of the watch' instead of giving a number of hours. The answer is that he wanted to teach that heaven has watches too, and at each one הקדוש ברוך הוא roars over the חורבן. The גמרא discusses the earthly signs for each watch, including one that tells a person in a dark room when to say the morning שמע. Then comes the story of רבי יוסי, who prayed in a ruin in ירושלים and learned three rules from אליהו. There he also heard a בת קול mourning the בית המקדש. The amud ends with a ברייתא giving three reasons not to enter a ruin, and the גמרא starts to question why the reason of suspicion is needed.

steps.title: רבי מאיר seems to contradict himself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that the two ברייתות give רבי מאיר two different start times for the evening שמע.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is a contradiction between one statement of רבי מאיר and another statement of רבי מאיר!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא notices that רבי מאיר is quoted two different ways and asks how that can be.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In one ברייתא, רבי מאיר says the time starts when the כהנים immerse before eating תרומה. In the other, he says it starts when people sit down to their Friday night meal. One person cannot hold two different start times, so the גמרא flags a contradiction.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Of X against X': the pattern for pointing out that one sage contradicts himself
Immersion in a מקוה, which the כהנים do before eating תרומה

steps.confusionAlert: Both start times come from ברייתות quoted just before this line. They are not in the משנה. The contradiction is between two outside teachings, both said in רבי מאיר's name.

phrases.english: There is a contradiction between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Meir!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the discussion by setting the two ברייתות quoted just before against each other.
steps.kashyaTarget: The consistency of רבי מאיר's opinion across two ברייתות
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One sage cannot give two different start times for the same מצוה.

steps.title: Two students reported רבי מאיר's view differently
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that two different תנאים passed down רבי מאיר's opinion in two different ways.
steps.simpleTranslation: Two תנאים reported the view of רבי מאיר differently.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא solves the contradiction by saying the two versions come from two different reporters, not from רבי מאיר changing his mind.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר himself held only one opinion. Two later תנאים disagreed about what that opinion was, and each ברייתא records one of their versions. So the contradiction is between the students, not inside רבי מאיר.

keyTerms.meaning: Two תנאים (sages of the משנה period)
'According to': reporting the view of a certain sage
A sage of the משנה period

steps.whyThisMatters: 'Two תנאים according to so-and-so' is a standard tool across ש״ס for explaining why one sage seems to say two different things.

phrases.english: Two tanna'im according to Rabbi Meir.
phrases.notes: He means two different sages each reported what רבי מאיר held, and they did not agree on it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Attributing the two versions to two different reporting תנאים
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי מאיר himself gave two conflicting start times.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי מאיר held one view. Two students disagreed about what it was.

steps.title: רבי אליעזר seems to contradict himself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that רבי אליעזר in the משנה and רבי אליעזר in the ברייתא give different start times.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is a contradiction between one statement of רבי אליעזר and another statement of רבי אליעזר!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises the same kind of problem again, this time about רבי אליעזר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In our משנה, רבי אליעזר seems to say the time starts when the כהנים go in to eat תרומה, which is when the stars come out. In the ברייתא, he says it starts when שבת begins on Friday night, which is earlier. Those two times are not the same.

keyTerms.meaning: A teaching of the תנאים that is not in the משנה
The portion of produce given to כהנים, which they may eat only once they are pure

phrases.english: There is a contradiction between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Eliezer!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Raises a second contradiction of the same type, now about רבי אליעזר.
steps.kashyaTarget: The consistency of רבי אליעזר's opinion between the משנה and the ברייתא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה and the ברייתא give רבי אליעזר two different start times for the evening שמע.

steps.title: Two answers: two reporters, or the first part is not רבי אליעזר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives two answers: either two תנאים reported רבי אליעזר differently, or the first part of the משנה is not his words at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: Two תנאים reported רבי אליעזר's view differently. Or, if you want, say that the first part of the משנה is not רבי אליעזר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers the same answer it gave for רבי מאיר, and then adds a second, different answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Answer one: two students passed down רבי אליעזר's view in two different ways. Answer two: the opening part of the משנה, about the כהנים eating תרומה, is a separate anonymous voice. רבי אליעזר only said the later part, 'until the end of the watch,' so there is no contradiction.

keyTerms.meaning: 'If you wish, say': introduces a second, alternative answer
The first part (opening clause) of a משנה or ברייתא
'It is not': this line does not belong to that sage

steps.confusionAlert: In the משנה, the words 'דברי רבי אליעזר' come at the end of the line, after both the start time and the end time. So it looks like both times are his. The second answer says his name applies only to the ending, 'until the end of the first watch,' and not to the start time before it.
steps.whatToRemember: Both רבי מאיר and רבי אליעזר can be explained with 'two תנאים.' For רבי אליעזר there is an extra option: the opening of the משנה is not his statement.

phrases.english: Two tanna'im according to Rabbi Eliezer,

phrases.aramaic: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: רֵישָׁא לָאו רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר הִיא.
phrases.english: and if you wish, say: the first clause is not Rabbi Eliezer.
phrases.notes: The 'first clause' is the משנה's opening start time, when the כהנים go in to eat תרומה.

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּרֵי תַּנָּאֵי אַלִּיבָּא דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר, וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction from step 3 with two possible solutions.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Two options: two reporting תנאים, or splitting who said which part of the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The whole line in the משנה, start time included, is רבי אליעזר's.
steps.terutzMaskana: Either the versions come from two different students, or רבי אליעזר said only 'until the end of the watch.'

steps.title: Quoting the משנה: until the end of the watch
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next words of the משנה, 'until the end of the watch,' to start a new discussion.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Until the end of the watch.'
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא quotes words from the משנה so it can explain them in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now that the start time is settled, the גמרא turns to the end time in רבי אליעזר's view. The next discussion will ask what a 'watch' is and how many watches the night has.

keyTerms.meaning: A 'watch': one section of the night

phrases.english: Until the end of the watch.
phrases.notes: These are רבי אליעזר's words in the משנה: the evening שמע may be said until the end of the first watch.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the start time to the end time in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי אליעזר rules that the evening שמע may be said until the end of the first watch. This sets up a discussion of what a 'watch' means.

steps.title: Why not just say the hour?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבי אליעזר uses the unclear word 'watch' when he could simply name an hour.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does רבי אליעזר hold? If he holds the night has three watches, let him say 'until four hours.' And if he holds the night has four watches, let him say 'until three hours'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי אליעזר's wording. Whatever he holds about how the night is divided, he could have just said a clear number of hours.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The night is twelve hours. With three watches, each watch is four hours, so he should say 'four hours.' With four watches, each is three hours, so he should say 'three hours.' Saying 'watch' leaves people unsure, so why did he pick that word?

keyTerms.meaning: Watches: the sections the night is divided into, like guard shifts
He holds / it is his opinion

phrases.english: What does Rabbi Eliezer hold?

phrases.aramaic: אִי קָסָבַר שָׁלֹשׁ מִשְׁמָרוֹת הָוֵי הַלַּיְלָה,
phrases.english: If he holds that the night is three watches,
let him say 'until four hours.'

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי קָסָבַר אַרְבַּע מִשְׁמָרוֹת הָוֵי הַלַּיְלָה,
phrases.english: And if he holds that the night is four watches,
let him say 'until three hours'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Picks up the משנה's words 'until the end of the watch' quoted in step 5 and questions them.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אליעזר's choice to measure the time in 'watches.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Under either way of dividing the night, a clear number of hours was available, so the word 'watch' looks needlessly vague.

steps.title: Watches in heaven and on earth
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר holds the night has three watches, and he says 'watch' to teach that there are watches in heaven too.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, he holds the night is three watches. And this is what he teaches us: there are watches in heaven and there are watches on earth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי אליעזר holds three watches, and he used the word 'watch' on purpose to teach an extra lesson.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He could have said 'four hours,' but the word 'watch' carries a message: the night is also divided into watches up in heaven. So the wording is not vague, it adds a teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: Really / actually: the גמרא keeps one of the options it raised
And this is what he is teaching us

phrases.aramaic: לְעוֹלָם קָסָבַר שָׁלֹשׁ מִשְׁמָרוֹת הָוֵי הַלַּיְלָה,
phrases.english: Really, he holds that the night is three watches,
and this is what he teaches us:
that there are watches in heaven
and there are watches on earth.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְעוֹלָם קָסָבַר שָׁלֹשׁ מִשְׁמָרוֹת הָוֵי הַלַּיְלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about why רבי אליעזר used the word 'watch.'
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the wording as deliberate, teaching an extra idea.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The word 'watch' was just an unclear way of giving the time.
steps.terutzMaskana: He holds three watches, and 'watch' was chosen to teach that heaven also has watches.

steps.title: הקדוש ברוך הוא roars at every watch
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא shows that רבי אליעזר himself spoke about three watches of the night in heaven.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא teaches: רבי אליעזר says, the night is three watches, and at each watch הקדוש ברוך הוא sits and roars like a lion, as the פסוק says: 'ה׳ roars from on high, from His holy dwelling He gives His voice, He roars mightily over His dwelling place.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא as support, showing that רבי אליעזר really did teach about watches in heaven.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this ברייתא, רבי אליעזר says outright that the night has three watches and that הקדוש ברוך הוא roars at each one. The פסוק is the source for the roaring. This confirms the answer in step 7.

keyTerms.meaning: The Holy One, Blessed be He

phrases.english: As it was taught: Rabbi Eliezer says:
The night is three watches,
and over each and every watch
the Holy One, Blessed be He, sits
and roars like a lion,
as it says: 'God roars from on high,'
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 25:30. The word 'roar' shows up three times in this פסוק, one for each watch.

phrases.english: 'and from His holy dwelling He gives His voice,'
'He roars mightily over His dwelling place.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer of step 7 with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that רבי אליעזר holds there are three watches in heaven.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא of רבי אליעזר, based on the פסוק in ירמיהו.

steps.title: Signs on earth for each watch
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues and gives a sign people can notice for each of the three watches.
steps.simpleTranslation: And a sign for this: in the first watch, a donkey brays; in the second, dogs bark; in the third, a baby nurses from its mother and a wife talks with her husband.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא keeps going and lists things that happen in our world to show when each heavenly watch changes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each watch has its own sound or event: donkeys, then dogs, then people starting to wake up. These signs let a person on earth tell which watch it is. This list sets up the question in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: A sign for the matter: a way to recognize it

phrases.english: And a sign for the matter:
the first watch, a donkey brays;
the second, dogs bark;
the third, a baby nurses from its mother's breast,
and a wife talks with her husband.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא, adding earthly signs for the watches.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each of the three watches has an earthly sign: donkey braying, dogs barking, baby nursing and wife talking with her husband.

steps.title: Start or end of the watches?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether the signs mark the start or the end of each watch, since either way one sign seems unneeded.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is רבי אליעזר counting? If he is counting the starts of the watches, why do I need a sign for the start of the first watch? It is evening! If he is counting the ends of the watches, why do I need a sign for the end of the last watch? It is day!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the list of signs. It sets up two choices and shows a problem with each one; the answer comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the signs mark when each watch begins, the first sign is wasted, because everyone knows the first watch starts at nightfall. If the signs mark when each watch ends, the last sign is wasted, because everyone knows the last watch ends when day comes. Either way, one sign seems pointless.
steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying the signs are wrong. It only asks which point in the watch they mark, since one sign always seems extra.

phrases.english: What is Rabbi Eliezer counting?
If he is counting the beginnings of the watches,

phrases.aramaic: תְּחִלַּת מִשְׁמָרָה רִאשׁוֹנָה סִימָנָא לְמָה לִי?
phrases.english: why do I need a sign for the beginning of the first watch?
It is evening!
If he is counting the ends of the watches,

phrases.aramaic: סוֹף מִשְׁמָרָה אַחֲרוֹנָה לְמָה לִי סִימָנָא?
phrases.english: why do I need a sign for the end of the last watch?
It is day!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the list of signs given in step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: The list of three signs in רבי אליעזר's ברייתא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Whether the signs mark the start or the end of each watch, one of the three signs marks something already obvious (nightfall or daybreak), so it seems unnecessary.

steps.title: The signs mark the hard-to-know moments of the night
steps.stepSummary: The signs are not all starts or all ends. They mark the end of the first watch, the start of the last watch, and the middle of the middle watch.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, he counted the end of the first watch, the beginning of the last watch, and the middle of the middle watch.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 10. The signs do not all mark the same point in their watch.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The start of the night and the end of the night are easy to notice, because it gets dark and then it gets light. So רבי אליעזר only gives signs for the moments you cannot see: the line between the first and middle watch, the line between the middle and last watch, and the middle of the night. This way no sign is wasted.

keyTerms.meaning: The middle of the middle watch

phrases.english: Rather, he counted
the end of the first watch,
and the beginning of the last watch,
and the middle of the middle watch.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the start-or-end question of Step 10
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation: the signs mark different points in different watches
steps.terutzHavaAmina: All the signs mark the same point, either all starts or all ends, so one sign is extra
steps.terutzMaskana: Each sign marks a moment that cannot be seen without it, so every sign is needed

steps.title: A second answer: all the signs mark the ends of the watches
steps.stepSummary: Another answer: every sign marks the end of its watch. The גמרא then raises the worry that the end of the last watch is obvious, since it is morning.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say: he is counting the ends of all the watches. And if you say the sign for the last one is not needed...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second answer: all three signs mark ends. It then repeats the old problem, that the end of the last watch is plain daylight, to set up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer goes back to the simple reading that the signs all mark ends. The words וכי תימא bring back the challenge: why do we need a sign for daybreak? The next step will answer that.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say (a second answer)
And if you say (an expected objection)

phrases.english: And if you want, say:
he is counting the ends of all the watches,
and if you say the last one is not needed...

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: כּוּלְּהוּ סוֹף מִשְׁמָרוֹת קָא חָשֵׁיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different answer to Step 10 and raises a problem with it
steps.terutzResolutionType: Alternative reading: all signs mark ends
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A sign for the end of the last watch is useless, because daylight already shows it
steps.terutzMaskana: All the signs mark ends; the usefulness of the last sign is explained in the next step

steps.title: Why we need a sign for the end of the night
steps.stepSummary: The last sign helps someone in a dark room who cannot see daybreak know when to say קריאת שמע.
steps.simpleTranslation: What difference does it make? It matters for reciting קריאת שמע, for someone who sleeps in a dark house and doesn't know when the time for קריאת שמע comes. Once a woman is talking with her husband and a baby is nursing from its mother, he should get up and recite.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the objection from Step 12. The sign for the end of the last watch is useful for a person who cannot see the sky.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Daylight is obvious only if you can see it. A person in a dark room needs another way to know morning has come. The household sounds of the last sign tell him it is time for the morning קריאת שמע.

keyTerms.meaning: What practical difference does it make?

steps.whatToRemember: Two answers to the signs question: (1) they mark the moments you cannot see, or (2) they all mark ends, and the last one helps a person in the dark know when to say קריאת שמע.

phrases.english: What difference does it make?
For reciting קריאת שמע
for someone who sleeps in a dark house

phrases.aramaic: וְלָא יָדַע זְמַן קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע אֵימַת.
phrases.english: and doesn't know when the time for קריאת שמע is.
Once a woman is talking with her husband
and a baby is nursing from its mother's breast,
he should get up and recite.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection raised at the end of Step 12
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The end of the night needs no sign because daylight shows it
steps.terutzMaskana: The sign is needed for someone in the dark, to know when to say קריאת שמע

steps.title: הקדוש ברוך הוא mourns at every watch of the night
steps.stepSummary: רב teaches that the night has three watches, and at each one הקדוש ברוך הוא roars like a lion over the destroyed בית המקדש and the exile.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יצחק בר שמואל said in the name of רב: The night has three watches. At each watch, הקדוש ברוך הוא sits and roars like a lion and says: 'Woe, that I destroyed My house, burned My Temple, and exiled My children among the nations of the world.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new statement that supports the idea of three watches in heaven. It tells what happens in heaven at each watch.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This connects to Step 7, where רבי אליעזר used the word 'watch' to hint at the watches in heaven. Here we learn what those heavenly watches are about: mourning over the חורבן. It also supports the view that the night has three watches, not four.
steps.whyThisMatters: It gives the heavenly watches from Step 7 a meaning: every part of the night is a time of mourning for the בית המקדש.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יִצְחָק בַּר שְׁמוּאֵל מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב:
phrases.english: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel said in the name of Rav:
The night has three watches,
and at each and every watch

phrases.aramaic: יוֹשֵׁב הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא וְשׁוֹאֵג כַּאֲרִי,
phrases.english: the Holy One, Blessed be He, sits and roars like a lion,
and says: 'Woe, that I destroyed My house,'
'and burned My Temple,'

phrases.aramaic: וְהִגְלֵיתִי אֶת בָּנַי לְבֵין אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם״.
phrases.english: 'and exiled My children among the nations of the world.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יִצְחָק בַּר שְׁמוּאֵל מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds an אגדה about the heavenly watches mentioned in Steps 7-8
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The night has three watches, and at each one הקדוש ברוך הוא mourns the חורבן and the exile

steps.title: רבי יוסי prays in a ruin and אליהו guards him
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא tells how רבי יוסי went into a ruin in ירושלים to pray, and אליהו guarded the doorway until he finished.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: רבי יוסי said: Once I was walking on the road, and I went into one of the ruins of ירושלים to pray. אליהו, may he be remembered for good, came and guarded the doorway for me until I finished my prayer.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a story, connected to the theme of mourning over ירושלים. This step sets the scene for the conversation that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story has no new rule yet. It sets up where רבי יוסי was and what he was doing. The lessons come out of the conversation with אליהו in the next steps.

keyTerms.meaning: May he be remembered for good

phrases.english: It was taught: Rabbi Yosei said:
Once I was walking on the road
and I went into a ruin,
one of the ruins of Jerusalem, to pray.
Elijah, may he be remembered for good, came
and guarded the doorway for me,
(and waited for me) until I finished my prayer.
phrases.notes: The words in round brackets are in the standard printed גמרא, but some versions leave them out.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי: פַּעַם אַחַת הָיִיתִי מְהַלֵּךְ בַּדֶּרֶךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A story connected to the mourning over ירושלים in Step 14
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Setup: רבי יוסי prayed in a ruin and אליהו guarded him

steps.title: אליהו asks why רבי יוסי went into the ruin
steps.stepSummary: After greeting each other, אליהו asks רבי יוסי why he entered the ruin, and רבי יוסי says it was to pray.
steps.simpleTranslation: After I finished my prayer, he said to me: 'Peace upon you, my teacher.' I said to him: 'Peace upon you, my teacher and my master.' He said to me: 'My son, why did you go into this ruin?' I said to him: 'To pray.'
steps.whatsHappening: אליהו and רבי יוסי greet each other, and אליהו asks a question. This sets up the lessons about going into ruins and where to pray.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question 'why did you go in?' hints that going into a ruin is a problem. רבי יוסי answers that he had a good reason, to pray. אליהו will now push on that reason.

phrases.english: After I finished my prayer, he said to me:
'Peace upon you, my teacher.'
And I said to him: 'Peace upon you, my teacher and my master.'
And he said to me: 'My son,'
'why did you go into this ruin?'
I said to him: 'To pray.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story right after the prayer
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why רבי יוסי went into the ruin

steps.title: אליהו: you should have prayed on the road
steps.stepSummary: אליהו challenges רבי יוסי's reason: he could have prayed on the road instead of going into a ruin.
steps.simpleTranslation: And he said to me: 'You should have prayed on the road.'
steps.whatsHappening: אליהו pushes back on רבי יוסי's answer. Praying is not a good enough reason to enter a ruin, since he could have prayed where he was.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי's reason was 'to pray'. אליהו points out that prayer does not need a ruin; the road was available. So there seems to be no need to go into the ruin.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר לִי: הָיָה לְךָ לְהִתְפַּלֵּל בַּדֶּרֶךְ.
phrases.english: And he said to me: 'You should have prayed on the road.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reason given in Step 16
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוסי's reason for entering the ruin
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Prayer could be done on the road, so there was no need to go into a ruin

steps.title: רבי יוסי was afraid of being interrupted
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי explains that on the road, passersby might have interrupted his prayer.
steps.simpleTranslation: And I said to him: 'I was afraid that travelers might interrupt me.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי defends himself against אליהו's challenge. He needed a quiet place so his prayer would not be broken.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The road had a problem: people passing by could disturb him in the middle of תפילה. So the ruin gave him privacy and focus.

phrases.english: And I said to him: 'I was afraid'
'that travelers might interrupt me,'

steps.triggerLanguage: מִתְיָרֵא הָיִיתִי שֶׁמָּא יַפְסִיקוּ בִּי עוֹבְרֵי דְּרָכִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אליהו's challenge in Step 17
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He could have simply prayed on the road
steps.terutzMaskana: On the road he would be interrupted, so he needed a quiet place

steps.title: אליהו: you should have said the short prayer
steps.stepSummary: אליהו rejects the answer: on the road he could have said the shortened תפילה made for such situations.
steps.simpleTranslation: And he said to me: 'You should have prayed a short prayer.'
steps.whatsHappening: אליהו rejects רבי יוסי's defense. Fear of interruption is solved by saying a short prayer, not by entering a ruin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי said the road was a problem because of interruptions. אליהו answers that there is a short תפילה for exactly this case, so he could pray quickly on the road. So the ruin was still not needed.

keyTerms.meaning: A short prayer, a shortened version of תפילה for hard situations

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר לִי הָיָה לְךָ לְהִתְפַּלֵּל תְּפִלָּה קְצָרָה.
phrases.english: And he said to me: 'You should have prayed a short prayer.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יוסי's defense from Step 18
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The claim that fear of interruption justified entering the ruin
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A short prayer on the road would have solved the problem of interruption

steps.title: Three lessons רבי יוסי learned from אליהו
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי lists the three rules he learned: don't enter a ruin, you may pray on the road, and on the road you say a short תפילה.
steps.simpleTranslation: At that moment I learned three things from him: one should not go into a ruin, one may pray on the road, and someone praying on the road says a short prayer.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי wraps up his conversation with אליהו by listing the three rules it taught him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each lesson comes from one move in the back-and-forth. אליהו's question showed that entering a ruin is wrong. His challenge showed that praying on the road is allowed. His rejection of רבי יוסי's answer showed that on the road you use the short תפילה.
steps.whatToRemember: Three rules: (1) don't enter a ruin, (2) you may pray on the road, (3) on the road you say a short תפילה.

phrases.aramaic: בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה לָמַדְתִּי מִמֶּנּוּ שְׁלֹשָׁה דְּבָרִים:
phrases.english: At that time I learned from him three things:
I learned that one may not enter a ruin,
and I learned that one may pray on the road,
and I learned that one who prays on the road
prays a short prayer.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה לָמַדְתִּי מִמֶּנּוּ שְׁלֹשָׁה דְּבָרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Summarizes the practical lessons from the exchange in steps 16-19
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Don't enter a ruin; you may pray on the road; on the road you say a short תפילה.

steps.title: אליהו asks what voice רבי יוסי heard
steps.stepSummary: אליהו asks רבי יוסי what voice he heard inside the ruin.
steps.simpleTranslation: And he said to me: My son, what voice did you hear in this ruin?
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues. אליהו asks a new question that sets up what רבי יוסי heard inside the ruin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story turns from rules about prayer to the mourning over the חורבן. אליהו's question sets up the description of the בת קול.

keyTerms.meaning: My son, a warm way of addressing someone

phrases.english: And he said to me: My son,
what voice did you hear in this ruin?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר לִי: בְּנִי, מָה קוֹל שָׁמַעְתָּ בְּחוּרְבָּה זוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves the story from the lessons on prayer to what רבי יוסי experienced in the ruin
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What sound רבי יוסי heard while praying in the ruin

steps.title: A heavenly voice mourning the destruction
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי heard a בת קול cooing like a dove, mourning that ה׳ destroyed His house, burned His היכל, and exiled His children.
steps.simpleTranslation: I said to him: I heard a heavenly voice cooing like a dove and saying, 'Woe, that I destroyed My house, burned My Temple, and exiled My children among the nations.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי answers אליהו by describing the mourning בת קול he heard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The voice speaks for ה׳, sad over the חורבן הבית and the גלות of His people. Like a dove's soft, sad cooing, it shows ה׳ mourning, not only punishing.

keyTerms.meaning: Cooing or moaning like a dove

phrases.english: And I said to him:

phrases.aramaic: שָׁמַעְתִּי בַּת קוֹל שֶׁמְּנַהֶמֶת כְּיוֹנָה וְאוֹמֶרֶת:
phrases.english: I heard a heavenly voice cooing like a dove and saying:
"Woe, that I destroyed My house
and burned My Temple

phrases.aramaic: וְהִגְלֵיתִי אֶת בָּנַי לְבֵין אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם״.
phrases.english: and exiled My children among the nations of the world."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אליהו's question from step 21
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He heard a בת קול mourning the destruction of the בית המקדש and the exile of ה׳'s children

steps.title: The mourning happens three times every day
steps.stepSummary: אליהו swears that this voice cries out not only at that moment but three times every day.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to me: By your life and your head, it doesn't say this only now; every single day it says this three times.
steps.whatsHappening: אליהו adds to what רבי יוסי heard: this mourning is not a one-time event but happens three times daily.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי may have thought he heard something rare. אליהו teaches that ה׳'s grief over the חורבן is constant and repeats every day.

keyTerms.meaning: By your life and your head, a strong way of swearing something is true

phrases.english: And he said to me: By your life and by the life of your head,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא שָׁעָה זוֹ בִּלְבַד אוֹמֶרֶת כָּךְ,
phrases.english: not only at this moment does it say this,
but every single day,
three times it says this.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands רבי יוסי's report into an ongoing daily reality
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ה׳'s mourning over the חורבן is heard three times every day.

steps.title: ה׳'s response when ישראל answer יהא שמיה הגדול מבורך
steps.stepSummary: When ישראל gather in בתי כנסיות and בתי מדרשות and answer 'יהא שמיה הגדול מבורך', ה׳ shakes His head, praising the king who is praised like this in his house, and grieving over the exiled children.
steps.simpleTranslation: Not only that: when Israel enter shuls and study halls and answer 'May His great name be blessed,' ה׳ shakes His head and says: Happy is the king who is praised like this in his house. What does the father have, who exiled his children? And woe to the children exiled from their father's table.
steps.whatsHappening: אליהו adds a second, even stronger point about ה׳'s feelings when ישראל praise Him in קדיש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The praise of 'יהא שמיה רבא' brings ה׳ joy, but it also reminds Him that this praise once happened in His own house, the בית המקדש. So the moment of praise is also a moment of grief, both for the Father and for the exiled children.

keyTerms.meaning: May His great name be blessed, the response in קדיש

steps.whatToRemember: ה׳ grieves over the חורבן three times a day, and even our praise in קדיש stirs both His joy and His sorrow.

phrases.english: And not only this, but

phrases.aramaic: בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁיִּשְׂרָאֵל נִכְנָסִין לְבָתֵּי כְּנֵסִיּוֹת וּלְבָתֵּי מִדְרָשׁוֹת
phrases.english: when Israel enters synagogues and study halls
and answers "May His great name be blessed,"

phrases.aramaic: הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְנַעְנֵעַ רֹאשׁוֹ, וְאוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: the Holy One, Blessed be He, shakes His head and says:

phrases.aramaic: אַשְׁרֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ שֶׁמְּקַלְּסִין אוֹתוֹ בְּבֵיתוֹ כָּךְ,
phrases.english: Happy is the king who is praised like this in his house;

phrases.aramaic: מַה לּוֹ לָאָב שֶׁהִגְלָה אֶת בָּנָיו,
phrases.english: what is there for the father who exiled his children,
phrases.notes: Literally 'what is there for him'; he means: how painful it is for this father.

phrases.aramaic: וְאוֹי לָהֶם לַבָּנִים שֶׁגָּלוּ מֵעַל שׁוּלְחַן אֲבִיהֶם.
phrases.english: and woe to the children who were exiled from their father's table.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a further example of ה׳'s ongoing grief, closing the story
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When ישראל answer יהא שמיה רבא‎, ה׳ rejoices in the praise and grieves over the exile.

steps.title: Three reasons not to enter a ruin
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא gives three reasons one may not go into a ruin: suspicion, collapse, and harmful spirits.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: For three reasons one may not enter a ruin: because of suspicion, because of collapse, and because of demons.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the first lesson, that one may not enter a ruin, and brings a ברייתא that explains why.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי only learned that entering a ruin is wrong. This ברייתא adds the reasons: people may suspect you, the building may fall on you, and מזיקין may live there. This sets up the questions that follow about each reason.

keyTerms.meaning: Suspicion, that people might suspect wrongdoing

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: for three reasons
one may not enter a ruin:

phrases.aramaic: מִפְּנֵי חֲשָׁד, מִפְּנֵי הַמַּפּוֹלֶת, וּמִפְּנֵי הַמַּזִּיקִין.
phrases.english: because of suspicion, because of collapse, and because of demons.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנָן, מִפְּנֵי שְׁלֹשָׁה דְּבָרִים אֵין נִכְנָסִין לְחוּרְבָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reasons behind the first lesson in step 20
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One may not enter a ruin because of suspicion, collapse, and demons.

steps.title: Why is suspicion needed if collapse is enough?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא lists suspicion, when the danger of collapse alone would already forbid entering.
steps.simpleTranslation: "Because of suspicion"? Why not just say the rule comes "because of collapse"?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא: one reason should be enough, so why list suspicion at all?
steps.deeperAnalysis: If danger of collapse already forbids entering every ruin, the reason of suspicion seems to add nothing. The גמרא is pushing to find a case where suspicion matters even when collapse is not a worry.

keyTerms.meaning: Let him get it from, meaning another reason already covers this

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying suspicion is false. It is asking why it needs to be listed, since collapse already seems to cover every case.

phrases.english: "Because of suspicion"
let him derive it instead "because of collapse"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the need for the first reason in the ברייתא of step 25
steps.kashyaTarget: The reason of חשד in the ברייתא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Collapse already forbids entering a ruin, so suspicion seems unnecessary
